title: Our Mutual Friend: A Literary Discussion

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked — a close, passionate, and occasionally contentious journey through one of the great novels of the English language.
Our Mutual Friend was Charles Dickens's last completed novel, published in 1864 and 1865, and it is — by any serious measure — among his most extraordinary achievements.
It is a novel obsessed with money: where it comes from, what it does to people, and what people will do to get it.
It is a novel about dust — literal dust heaps that constitute a vast fortune — and about resurrection: bodies pulled from the Thames, identities shed and reclaimed.
To help us unpack all of this, I am joined today by three extraordinary readers of this novel, and I want to introduce each of them properly.
Oliver Trevelyan is an actor, writer, and the voice behind more classic novel audiobooks than perhaps anyone alive.
He comes to every novel as a performer first — which means he hears things in the prose that the rest of us miss on the page.
Dr Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads novels as anatomies of class and power.
He will tell us what the money actually means — and who pays for it.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read this novel as a teenager and has returned to it many times since.
She brings the reader's eye — attentive to what moves you, what makes you laugh, and what makes you stop and re-read a sentence.
Let's begin at the beginning — or rather, at the heart of it: money, its inheritance, and the damage it does before a single coin changes hands.
What strikes me most forcefully about this novel — from the very first pages — is that its central fortune is built on filth.
The dust heaps are refuse, waste, the discarded matter of a city — and yet they represent fabulous wealth.
Dickens is telling us, right from the outset, exactly where capital comes from.
And what's remarkable is that John Harmon — the heir to all this — already knows it, already feels it, before he even claims the inheritance.
There is a passage in which Harmon, in his disguise, works through his own moral situation — and it is devastating in its clarity.
He says: "I came back, shrinking from my father's money, shrinking from my father's memory, mistrustful of being forced on a mercenary wife."
Every repetition of that word — shrinking — is doing enormous work.
He is not simply reluctant to inherit — he is physically recoiling from what the money represents.
That passage is extraordinary to read aloud — the rhythm of it is almost liturgical.
"Shrinking from my father's money, shrinking from my father's memory" — Dickens is doing something very close to incantation there.
And then it breaks — "now, stop, and so far think it out, John Harmon" — which is Harmon actually speaking to himself.
He is interrogating his own consciousness in real time — and the novel lets us watch it happen.
Now — Dickens being Dickens — he will not let money remain tragic for long before finding its comic obverse.
Because alongside the tortured Harmon, we have Silas Wegg — a man of wooden leg and boundless cupidity — and Wegg's relationship with money is pure farce.
There is a scene in which Wegg, caught up in excitement over a revelation of hidden wealth, simply topples over onto Mr Venus.
And Dickens describes both of them as — "remaining in a kind of pecuniary swoon."
"Pecuniary swoon" — two words, and you've got the whole grotesque comedy of greed in a single image.
What I love about that Wegg passage — and what I think Daniel's reading of Harmon deepens — is the contrast Dickens holds in tension throughout this novel.
Money destroys Harmon's inner life before he has even touched it.
And money reduces Wegg — already a figure of comic degradation — to a state of physical helplessness.
It's the same force, operating at different registers — tragic in one key, farcical in another.
And then there's the passage with Wegg at the keyhole — which I find genuinely unsettling.
Dickens writes that Wegg "laboured with a will at turning an imaginary grindstone outside the keyhole, while Mr Boffin stooped at it within."
It is pantomime, yes — but it is also a mime of domination.
The grindstone is imaginary, but the power Wegg holds over Boffin is entirely real — and Dickens catches both things simultaneously.
Caroline is exactly right, and I want to press that point further.
Wegg is a blackmailer — a man with no capital except information — and the keyhole scene shows us class power running, briefly, in reverse.
The rich man stoops; the poor man grinds.
But Dickens makes it grotesque and comic rather than triumphant — which tells us something about the limits of his radicalism.
The system is not overturned — it is briefly mocked, and then Wegg stumps home.
What stays with me, though, is the figure of Eugene Wrayburn — a man of privilege so complete it has become a kind of paralysis.
There is a passage in which the wretched figure of Jenny Wren's father shuffles past Eugene — and Dickens describes him as:
"The miserable man, feebly rubbing the back of his faltering hands downward from the wrists, shuffled on to his post of disgrace."
And Eugene barely notices him — "instinctively falling away from the disagreeable contact" — before lighting his cigar and departing.
Poverty, in this novel, is something the comfortable classes fall away from — reflexively, without thought.
That cigar is doing a great deal of work, isn't it.
Eugene lights it and departs — that is the entirety of his moral engagement with the wretchedness in front of him.
Dickens writes the idle classes with a very cold eye — warmer for the Weggs and Venuses of the world, in a perverse way.
At least Wegg wants something desperately — he is alive to money in his bones.
Eugene's indifference is a more refined kind of corruption.
Money as inheritance, as farce, as paralysis — we've already mapped some of the novel's central tensions in the space of a few passages.
And we haven't yet touched the Thames, the dust heaps, or the extraordinary web of characters Dickens weaves around them.
In our next segment, we turn to the novel's great theme of resurrection — identity lost and remade — and what that means for nearly every character in this book.

segments.title: The Harmon Riddle: Who Is Dead?

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's last completed novel seriously — and with great pleasure.
I'm your host, and today we're opening with the riddle at the heart of the whole novel: who, exactly, is dead?
A body pulled from the Thames, an identity in question, a fortune in the balance — and Dickens, characteristically, playing every card close to his chest.
To think through this riddle, I'm joined by three brilliant readers.
Oliver Trevelyan has narrated more classic novels than perhaps anyone alive — he hears Dickens the way a musician hears a score.
Dr Daniel Rosen reads the novel as a map of class power, and he will not let us forget what the Harmon fortune costs the people at the bottom.
And Caroline Woodcourt is the reader who has lived with this book the longest — she knows every sentence, and she cares about every character.
Let's begin with what Dickens himself admitted about the central deception.
He was quite direct about it, in a postscript that is really one of the more remarkable authorial confessions in Victorian fiction.
What's extraordinary about that postscript is that Dickens essentially turns to the audience and says: yes, I know you guessed it.
And he's not embarrassed.
He's almost amused.
He writes — and this is from the postscript itself — that he foresaw the likelihood of readers supposing he was concealing the very thing he was suggesting.

"I foresaw the likelihood that a class of readers and commentators would suppose that I was at great pains to conceal exactly what I was at great pains to suggest: namely, that Mr John Harmon was not slain, and that Mr John Rokesmith was he."
That's a conjuror winking at the audience before the trick is even finished.
He's telling us the sleight of hand was always transparent — and that the transparency was the point.
And what's so pointed about that passage is the language he uses: a class of readers.
Dickens can't even describe his readership without the word class slipping in.
But I'd push further than Oliver on this.
The fact that Harmon's identity is in question for so long isn't just a plot puzzle — it's the novel's central anxiety about what identity is made of.
Who is John Harmon? He's the heir to dust mounds and refuse — literally built from what the city throws away.
The fortune that defines him is a fortune made from other people's waste.
What I keep returning to is what happens to that identity in the hands of the Boffins.
Because there's a passage where Mr Boffin describes standing up for young John against his monstrous father — time after time.
And Dickens doesn't let it stay abstract.
He gives us this extraordinary, absurd, heartbreaking image of Mrs Boffin's bonnet being knocked off her head.

"I have seen him, after Mrs Boffin has given him her mind respecting the claims of the nat'ral affections, catch off Mrs Boffin's bonnet (she wore, in general, a black straw, perched as a matter of convenience on the top of her head), and send it spinning across the yard."
And then — and this is where Dickens earns your full attention — he lands it.
"Which dropped her, Mr Lightwood. Dropped her."
Two words, repeated.
All the violence of Old Harmon's world compressed into those two words.
That repetition is pure performance.
Boffin pauses before the second 'Dropped her' — you can hear it, even on the page.
He's not reporting what happened.
He's making Mortimer Lightwood — and through him, us — feel the weight of it.
And the comic detail of the black straw bonnet 'perched as a matter of convenience' — that's Dickens trusting the comedy to carry the tragedy.
He doesn't choose between them.
And that loyalty — the Boffins' loyalty to young John against his own father — is what makes the inheritance so morally loaded.
They didn't expect a penny of it.
And when it falls to them anyway — because the heir is apparently dead — Mrs Boffin's first instinct isn't acquisition.
It's to find an orphan child and rename him after the boy they lost.
"Now that he is past all benefit of the money, and it's come to us, I should like to find some orphan child, and take the boy and adopt him and give him John's name, and provide for him."
There is something almost liturgical in that impulse.
The money cannot resurrect John Harmon, so you redeem it by giving a different child his name and his future.
The Boffins are doing with capital what capital almost never does: turning it back toward the people it took everything from.
That line 'Somehow, it would make me easier, I fancy' is the one that undoes me every time.
She's not claiming virtue.
She's not making a moral argument.
She's just describing a grief that needs somewhere to go.
And of course the irony that Dickens is building, silently, is that John Harmon is alive — and watching all of this.
He is the orphan the Boffins are trying to replace — with himself.
That's the most Gothic thing in the whole novel and it's dressed in the warmest possible clothes.
Now, identity and disguise in Our Mutual Friend don't stop at Harmon.
There's another figure in the novel who takes disguise to a genuinely chilling place — Bradley Headstone, dressing as a bargeman to destroy Eugene Wrayburn.
And what's so theatrically satisfying — if that's the right word — is that he gets caught not by deduction, but by a witness who was playing exactly the same game.
Riderhood watched every move.
"I've got your Bargeman's clothes, tore this way and that way with the scuffle, stained green with the grass, and spattered all over with what bust from the blows. I've got them, and I've got you."
Every disguise in this novel leaves a stain.
Literally, in this case.
What Riderhood's speech reveals is that the whole logic of disguise in this novel is class performance.
Headstone dresses down — puts on the bargeman's clothes — to move through a world below his station and commit violence without accountability.
Harmon dresses down as Rokesmith — the meek secretary — to observe the world he's entitled to inherit.
In both cases, the disguise is a way of escaping the obligations that come with your assigned place in the class structure.
The difference is that Harmon uses his freedom to fall in love.
Headstone uses his to try to commit murder.
And the novel punishes Headstone for it, with a kind of operatic inevitability.

What I find remarkable is how Dickens threads all of this — Harmon's concealed identity, the Boffins' grief, the violence beneath the surface — into a novel that still feels, in long stretches, like a comedy.
In our next segment, we'll look at the people who have no disguise to wear — those at the very bottom of this world, for whom identity is not a puzzle but a sentence.
Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
Today we're going deep into the novel's most unsettling preoccupation: what money does to people from the inside.
Dickens gives us Bella Wilfer as his central experiment — a young woman who knows her own greed and is half-ashamed of it.
But he also gives us a whole social world built on the same hunger — dressed up in dinner tables and respectability.
With me are Oliver Trevelyan, actor and audiobook narrator — a man who has made Dickens's prose sound like music for thirty years.
Daniel Rosen, cultural historian, who reads every social institution in the novel as a machine for keeping people in their place.
And Caroline Woodcourt, critic and reader, whose feeling for what's funny and what's heartbreaking in these pages is unmatched.
Daniel, let's start with you — and with a figure who might seem peripheral but who I think unlocks the whole social comedy of the novel.
Tell us about Twemlow.
Twemlow is one of Dickens's most devastating comic inventions — and the key to understanding everything else in this novel.
He is not merely a comic butt. He is a precise diagram of how social value is extracted from human beings.
Dickens calls him, without irony, 'an innocent piece of dinner-furniture that went upon easy castors.'
'Being first cousin to Lord Snigsworth, he was in frequent requisition, and at many houses might be said to represent the dining-table in its normal state.'
He is literally reduced to furniture. His aristocratic connection is the hinge on which his entire social existence turns.
And what I find so precise here is the geometry: the more guests are added, the further Twemlow is pushed from the centre.
His social utility increases — and his social dignity decreases — in exact proportion.
What I love about that passage is that Dickens is performing the very thing he's describing.
The prose itself extends outward — the sentences get longer, the clauses accumulate — just as Twemlow is pulled out to his twenty leaves.
When I read it aloud, there's an extraordinary comic rhythm to it. You feel the mechanical stretch in the syntax.
And 'easy castors' — that detail is perfect. It tells you Twemlow is conveniently portable. He offers no resistance.
And yet — and this is what moves me about Twemlow — Dickens never lets us fully laugh at him.
He is described as 'innocent.' That word does real work. It means he has not chosen this. It has simply happened to him.
And being kept 'over a livery stable-yard in Duke Street' when not in use — he is stored, like furniture.
There's something genuinely sad in that detail, even inside the comedy.
Exactly — and that's the template Dickens is establishing before we meet Bella, before we meet the Boffins, before we see what wealth does to everyone it touches.
The Veneerings use Twemlow as social capital. He is currency. He is already what Bella fears she might become — a person valued entirely for their utility to others.
That's a fascinating pivot. Because Bella, unlike Twemlow, knows what's happening to her.
She watches herself in the mirror. She interrogates herself. And the result is one of the novel's most startling passages of self-examination.
Daniel, you've been looking closely at the scene where Bella comes back to her room after talking with the Boffins.
This is, for me, the most psychologically penetrating moment in the entire novel.
Boffin has been preaching the gospel of money — its comfort, its wisdom, its inevitability.
And Bella agrees. She agrees entirely. The trouble is she cannot bear herself for agreeing.
Listen to how Dickens renders her interior monologue. She's standing at the looking-glass, interrogating herself:
'Why, what need to excuse him? What he said was very sensible, I am sure, and very true, I am sure.'
'It is only what I often say to myself. Don't I like it then? No, I don't like it, and, though he is my liberal benefactor, I disparage him for it.'
'Then pray, what do you mean by this, you inconsistent little Beast?'
That word — 'Beast' — is Bella calling herself out with a ferocity that no other character in the novel can manage about themselves.
She sees the contradiction, names it, and cannot resolve it. That is the most honest thing in the book.
When I read that passage for the recording, I had to stop after 'inconsistent little Beast' and just sit with it.
Because it's written entirely in Bella's voice. Not the narrator's voice. Hers.
Dickens has surrendered the text to her. And what she says is funnier and more damning than anything he could say about her.
Performatively, the challenge is the repetition — 'I am sure, and very true, I am sure.' You have to honour the rhythm without sending it up.
Because she's not being comic. She's being brutal with herself. And that distinction is everything.
What strikes me is that the looking-glass becomes her confessional throughout this novel.
She can say things to her reflection that she can't say to anyone else. It's the one space of honesty she has.
And 'inconsistent' is the crucial word. Not wicked. Not vain. Inconsistent.
She wants to be better than her desires. That tension is what makes her worth four hundred pages.
Now, Bella's story exists alongside characters for whom the question of gold is not philosophical but entirely material.
Caroline, there's a passage involving Lizzie Hexam and little Jenny Wren that I think belongs in this conversation — even though its subject is care rather than money.
This scene is one of the most beautiful things in the entire novel, and it almost stops the plot entirely to offer something else.
Lizzie is brushing out Jenny Wren's long fair hair — it's their evening ritual when they're alone together.
And Dickens writes, of the hair falling free:
'it fell in a beautiful shower over the poor shoulders that were much in need of such adorning rain.'
'Adorning rain.' Two words. Doing the work of a whole paragraph of sentiment without sentimentality.
The beauty is given freely to someone who has known very little of it. That is what the sentence holds.
And then it reverses. Jenny loosens Lizzie's dark hair in return — 'it dropped of its own weight over her bosom, in two rich masses.'
The exchange is entirely equal. Neither woman is the giver, neither the receiver.
In a novel obsessed with who owes whom, that mutuality is almost radical.
I'd go further. In a novel where every relationship has a price — Twemlow's connections, Bella's inheritance, Riderhood's blackmail — this scene is almost the only one that costs nothing.
But notice what surrounds it. Lizzie comes from the world Dickens describes elsewhere in the novel — families destroyed by drink, children born into degradation.
There's a line — a devastating one — about a child Lizzie knows:
'This poor ailing little creature has come to be what she is, surrounded by drunken people from her cradle — if she ever had one, Charley.'
'If she ever had one.' That parenthetical — almost thrown away — is the most quietly terrible thing in those pages.
Bella's question about whether she deserves wealth has to be held against that image. The stakes are not merely moral. They are social.
That line always stops me cold on re-reading.
Because it's Lizzie speaking, and Lizzie herself came from that world. She knows exactly what she's describing.
And she describes it without self-pity. Without drama. That restraint is its own kind of eloquence.
The novel also has its counter-image of this social world — in its bleakest corner: the river, and what it gives back.
Daniel, let's talk about Gaffer Hexam's end — and what that stark little moment says about the logic of the world Dickens has built.
Gaffer Hexam lives by the river — by scavenging from its dead. It's a grotesque economy, but it follows its own pitiless logic.
And then the river takes him. He becomes what he harvested.
Riderhood's response — when he recognises the body — is just four words. Four words that contain everything:
'Gaffer's done me. It's Gaffer!'
His first response to a man's death is not grief. Not horror. It's the recognition that he has been cheated — that the enemy escaped by dying.
These are people for whom death is an economic event. There is no softening in Dickens here. None.
And yet there's something almost classical in it. Greek, almost — the river as fate, as the thing that gives and reclaims.
Dickens strips all the sentiment out and gives you the bare transaction. And that bareness is its own kind of power.
As a performer you don't emote that line. You deliver it flat. The flatness is the horror.
That note of inescapable consequence brings us to our final passage for today — and to Bradley Headstone, a man trapped by his own guilt.
Daniel, the narrator does something remarkable with Bradley — a kind of forensic analysis of how the criminal mind deceives itself.
Bradley Headstone is the novel's most psychologically modern figure. He is the self-made man who has made himself into a catastrophe.
And here, after the violence, Dickens gives us a generalisation that reads almost like a law of nature:
'There are fifty doors by which discovery may enter. With infinite pains and cunning, he double locks and bars forty-nine of them, and cannot see the fiftieth standing wide open.'
Guilt works as a kind of cognitive blindness. The harder Bradley works to cover his tracks, the less he can perceive the real danger.
Riderhood — whom he has controlled, used, instrumentalised — is the fiftieth door. Standing wide open. And Bradley cannot see it.
That metaphor of the doors — I've read it dozens of times and it still lands with the force of inevitability.
There's something almost mathematical in how Dickens constructs it. Forty-nine. One. The precision makes it merciless.
And 'wide open' — not ajar, not cracked — wide open. The threat isn't hidden. Bradley simply cannot see it.
What's remarkable about that passage is how the narrator steps outside the story entirely to deliver a verdict.
'And this is another spell against which the shedder of blood for ever strives in vain.' 'For ever.' Not just Bradley — every guilty man, in every story.
It's one of those moments when Dickens is clearly reaching past the novel — speaking to the reader, across time.
And somehow it never feels like a digression. It feels inevitable.
And that word — inevitable — feels like the right note on which to pause today.
Bella calls herself a Beast and cannot understand why. Bradley bars forty-nine doors and leaves the fiftieth open.
Twemlow is stored over a livery stable-yard and has never once complained.
This novel keeps asking: what does wanting money — or simply living inside the system that distributes it — do to a person?
We haven't finished with that question. We'll continue in our next segment.
My thanks to Oliver Trevelyan, Daniel Rosen, and Caroline Woodcourt for an extraordinary conversation.

segments.title: The Wit and Warmth of Dickens's Voice

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's last completed novel seriously — and joyfully.
Our Mutual Friend is a novel of surfaces and secrets, of money and mud, of brilliant comic invention sitting right alongside genuine darkness.
Today we begin with something that might seem obvious but is actually quite profound: the question of what Dickens's voice actually does to a reader.
With me are three wonderful companions for this journey.
Oliver Trevelyan has narrated more classic novels than perhaps anyone alive, and he brings a performer's ear to every sentence — he hears what the prose is actually doing.
Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian whose readings of Dickens are always alert to the mechanisms of power hidden inside even the funniest scenes.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a critic and lifelong reader of this novel, someone who came to it as a teenager and has never quite left it.
Oliver, let's begin with you — because I think no one is better placed to talk about the sheer pleasure of Dickens's comic voice in this novel.
The first thing you notice, reading this novel aloud — and I mean actually aloud — is how much Dickens trusts silence.
He sets up a joke and then leaves a gap — a syntactical gap — for the audience to fall into.
The Lammle scenes are a perfect example of this.
We're watching this couple perform tender affection for their guests, and Dickens is watching them watching themselves.
And then comes this extraordinary line — he just punctures the whole scene with what I can only call gleeful menace.
"How delightful those interchanges, and the looks accompanying them! Now, if the skeleton up-stairs had taken that opportunity, for instance, of calling out 'Here I am, suffocating in the closet!'"
The word 'suffocating' — I defy anyone to read that without a shiver of delight.
It's grotesque and funny and genuinely unsettling all at once — which is Dickens at full stretch.
What strikes me about that passage is the narrator's complicity with the reader.
He's saying: you and I both know what's really happening here, even if no one in the room does.
The skeleton is an almost too-perfect metaphor — except Dickens doesn't let it be a metaphor.
He personifies it. He gives it a voice. He makes it knock from inside the closet.
That's the thing about re-reading this novel — I've read it four or five times and I still stop at that sentence.
I want to pick up on something Oliver said about the gap — the silence that Dickens leaves.
Because what the Lammles are performing is not just affection — it is credit.
The tenderness between them is a form of financial solvency — it's the performance that keeps their social world believing in them.
And that skeleton in the closet is not just secrets — it is debt.
The fraud they're concealing is the structural condition of their entire existence in this novel.
And Dickens makes it funny — which is, I think, one of the radical things about how he works.
Daniel's absolutely right that the comedy is doing serious work — but I want to stay with the comic mechanism for a moment longer.
Because the Lammle–Fledgeby confrontation takes this to a completely different pitch.
Lammle puffs himself up to his full chest and delivers this magnificent tirade.
The stage direction is right there in the prose: 'making the most of his chest.'

"This fellow presumes on my having in my desk round the corner, his dirty note of hand for a wretched sum payable on the occurrence of a certain event, which event can only be of my and my wife's bringing about!"
The rhythm of that — 'this fellow, Fledgeby, presumes to be impertinent to me, Lammle' — is pure music-hall.
And then: 'Give me your nose, sir.' Three words. The whole thing collapses into farce.
'Give me your nose, sir' — I laughed out loud the first time I read that, and I still do.
But what I find interesting is how Dickens distributes this kind of comic energy across the novel.
Because it's not just in the drawing-room satire — it shows up in the most unlikely places.
When Harmon finally catches up with Wegg and grabs him by the cravat — that moment is written as pure slapstick.
'Shaken until his teeth chattered' — you can hear the rattling.

"Wegg had repeated the word with a sneer, and was entering on some sarcastic retort, when, to his boundless amazement, he found himself gripped by the cravat; shaken until his teeth chattered; shoved back, staggering, into a corner of the room; and pinned there."
The semi-colons do all the work — each blow lands separately, metrically.
And Wegg deserves every one of those blows — let's be honest.
But what that scene dramatises is the return of legitimate property — Harmon reasserting his right against a man who has been pilfering and scheming.
Dickens makes it feel like justice because it's physical, immediate, visceral.
But the comic energy is also — and I say this with some care — a kind of release valve.
It lets us enjoy the catharsis without having to think too hard about what the system that produced Wegg actually looks like.
I think Daniel's right, and I want to come at it from a different angle — the moment in this novel where Dickens's voice shifts entirely.
The John Harmon confession passage is unlike almost anything else in the novel.
All that comic propulsion just stops. And we go somewhere very dark and very strange.
When I recorded it, I had to find a completely different register — slower, more disoriented.
Listen to what Harmon says about the moment he loses himself entirely:

"I saw a figure like myself lying dressed in my clothes on a bed. What might have been, for anything I knew, a silence of days, weeks, months, years, was broken by a violent wrestling of men all over the room."
'A silence of days, weeks, months, years' — he doesn't know how long he was gone.
Identity, time, the body itself — all of it dissolves. That's not comedy. That's something much older.
That passage stops me every time.
The accumulation of passives — 'I was turned over,' 'I was dragged,' 'I was trodden upon' — Harmon is entirely without agency.
He is a thing being acted upon, not a person acting.
And that strange detail — hearing the blows and thinking of a wood-cutter in a forest — is genuinely hallucinatory.
It's a completely different register from the Lammle scenes, and yet it's the same novel, the same voice.
And I think that range — from the skeleton suffocating in the closet to John Harmon dissolving into nothing — is exactly what makes this novel so hard to characterise.
Dickens's voice is not one thing. It never was.
Coming up, we'll look more closely at what that voice does to the world it portrays — specifically, the world of money, class, and who gets to survive in it.

segments.title: Boffin's Gambit: Class, Corruption, and the Dust Heaps

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the podcast that takes one of Dickens's greatest and most unjustly overlooked novels apart — and puts it back together with fresh eyes.

I'm your host, and today we're digging into one of the novel's most fascinating moral puzzles: the Boffins, the dust heaps, and what it means to be genuinely good in a world where money corrupts everything it touches.
With me today are three exceptional readers of this novel.

Oliver Trevelyan has voiced more classic novels than anyone alive, and he comes to Dickens as a performer first — hearing the rhythms, catching the comic timing, feeling where the prose wants to breathe.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads every novel as an anatomy of class power — and in Our Mutual Friend, he has extraordinarily rich material to work with.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived with this novel since her teenage years and brings an intimate, emotionally attuned reading that catches what the others might stride past.
Let's begin with old John Harmon — the dead miser — and the extraordinary trust he placed in the Boffins.
What strikes me every time I return to the passage about old Harmon's will is how Dickens gives us a miser who is morally self-aware and utterly unable to act on that awareness.
He knows the Boffins are honest. He rages at them for it. And yet — he writes their names in his will.
Dickens puts it with such concentrated precision — let me read the line.
"he had perceived the powerlessness of all his wealth to buy them if he had addressed himself to the attempt."
That word — powerlessness — is doing so much work.
The entire novel circles around the question of what money can and cannot purchase, and here it is, stated outright in the very opening of the Boffin story.
Caroline is right that the line is remarkable — but I want to press on what Dickens is doing ideologically when he frames virtue this way.
Old Harmon is described as a 'griping taskmaster' who 'mistrusted all mankind' — and Dickens adds the devastating qualifier that he especially mistrusted those 'who bore any resemblance to himself.'
So the miser knows he is corrupt. He recognises incorruptibility when he sees it precisely because he has spent his life trying to corrupt others.
What troubles me is this: Dickens uses the Boffins' integrity to redeem the system — to suggest that honest servants can inherit and steward a fortune built on the labour of the poor.
The dust heaps themselves — the source of all this wealth — were worked by people we never name in the novel.
Daniel, you are absolutely right that the dust heaps have their ghostly workforce — but I think Dickens is playing a more complicated game than simple redemption.
The Boffins are set up as paragons — but then the novel immediately surrounds them with a magnificent carnival of human greed.
There is a passage — the taxonomy of beggars writing to Boffin for money — which is, I would argue, one of the great comic set-pieces in all of Dickens.
The narrator says of their letters — and I must read this —
"they call their scraps documents; but they are, as to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf."
Minced veal to a calf. The man was a genius.
The comedy is lacerating — but notice how it also makes the beggars ridiculous rather than pitiable, which is where I think Daniel's unease is entirely warranted.
Yes — and Oliver puts his finger on exactly the problem.
That passage is a masterpiece of satirical taxonomy, but who is being satirised?
The desperate. The indebted. The woman writing secretly from her husband because they are both too ashamed to acknowledge they are ruined.
Dickens shows them reaching upward toward sudden, unearned wealth — the same wealth the Boffins themselves received — and makes us laugh at them for it.
The novel is, in those moments, doing ideological work on behalf of the class it pretends to interrogate.
I hear both of you — and I think you're both right, which is part of what makes this novel so uncomfortable to sit with.
But I want to turn to something that throws the whole Boffin question into a different light — the moment when John Harmon finally speaks his gratitude.
He is confronting Wegg — furious, barely contained — and he says, addressing himself to the accusation that he holds the fortune by right:
"I owe everything I possess, solely to the disinterestedness, uprightness, tenderness, goodness (there are no words to satisfy me) of Mr and Mrs Boffin."
That parenthesis — 'there are no words to satisfy me' — is one of the most quietly devastating moments in the book.
Language fails at genuine virtue. And Dickens has the courage to say so, right there in the sentence.
That is a beautiful observation, Caroline — and as someone who has read that speech aloud many times, I can tell you the parenthesis is almost impossible to render without emotion.
Harmon is a man who has spent the entire novel concealing his identity, measuring everyone around him — including the Boffins — for trustworthiness.
And then Wegg — this magnificent, self-serving grotesque — dares to presume against them, and something breaks open in Harmon.
The novel needs Wegg precisely so that this moment can happen — so that virtue can be named, violently defended, in the heat of real anger.
Before we leave the question of class and appearance entirely, I cannot let go of Sloppy.
Because Sloppy in his new black suit is — if you will allow me — one of the finest comic descriptions of a human body in any Dickens novel.
Oh, I was hoping we'd get to Sloppy.
The tailor has been instructed to deploy 'the utmost cunning of his art' to conceal Sloppy's buttons. The buttons win.
Dickens writes — and this is the passage I always return to —
"he now stood before the Council, a perfect Argus in the way of buttons: shining and winking and gleaming and twinkling out of a hundred of those eyes of bright metal, at the dazzled spectators."
'The dazzled spectators.' He makes us complicit in the comedy — we are the spectators.
But Sloppy is also a figure of genuine goodness in this novel — his body is uncontainable, and so, in a different way, is his heart.
And that is exactly where the novel's politics become most interesting to me — in bodies like Sloppy's.
The suit is Mrs Boffin's charity — a gift of black cloth that cannot disguise what Sloppy is, where he comes from, or what his body has been shaped by.
Tailoring science — those are Dickens's words — cannot contain the frailties of his form.
Class is written on the body. Philanthropy can dress it, but cannot rewrite it.
And yet — as Caroline says — the novel loves Sloppy. That tension is never resolved. I find that more honest than a resolution would be.
Before we move on, I have to note that the novel doesn't let us rest in the warmth of the Boffins and Sloppy for long.

Because shadowing the whole novel is Bradley Headstone — and there is a passage of almost unbearable gothic intensity that belongs in this conversation about what wealth, and the lack of it, does to a person.
Bradley sitting before the fire all night, in Riderhood's grip — Dickens writes it like this:

"Rigid before the fire, as if it were a charmed flame that was turning him old, he sat, with the dark lines deepening in his face, its stare becoming more and more haggard, its surface turning whiter and whiter as if it were being overspread with ashes, and the very texture and colour of his hair degenerating."
A charmed flame that was turning him old. That is the sentence of a poet.
From the comic buttons of Sloppy's suit to the ashes spreading across Bradley Headstone's face — that range is everything.
The Boffins sit at the moral centre of this novel as a kind of impossible exception — honest souls in a system designed to corrupt.
And as Daniel reminds us, the novel is not entirely comfortable with its own optimism about them — which may be precisely why it endures.
In our next segment, we'll be looking at the river — the Thames as both graveyard and marketplace — and what it reveals about the lives of those who work it.

segments.title: Reading the Room: Dickens's Comedy of Manners

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
We've been exploring this extraordinary novel across its many registers — tragic, satirical, tender, grotesque.
In this segment we're turning to what Dickens does perhaps better than anyone — the comedy of social pretension.
But we're also sitting with the novel's moral centre — John Harmon's extraordinary act of self-erasure in the name of love.
With me, as ever, are Oliver Trevelyan, Daniel Rosen, and Caroline Woodcourt.
The passages we're dealing with today are ones I find myself returning to every time I re-read the book.
Because Dickens is playing two very different instruments simultaneously — biting satire in one hand, genuine moral weight in the other.
Take Mr Boffin on charitable patronage — this is Dickens at his most gleefully unhinged.

'Patrons and Patronesses, and Vice-Patrons and Vice-Patronesses, and Deceased Patrons and Deceased Patronesses, and Ex-Vice-Patrons and Ex-Vice-Patronesses, what does it all mean in the books of the Charities that come pouring in on Rokesmith as he sits among 'em pretty well up to his neck!'
The accumulation of titles — each one slightly more absurd than the last — that's not just a joke, that's a musical composition.
You have to perform it. The moment you read it aloud you hear Dickens grinning behind the page.
And the grin is backed by something fierce, which is what makes Boffin's rant genuinely radical rather than merely amusing.
Five shillings buys you a Patroness title. Five shillings — the price of appearing virtuous to your social circle.
Boffin calls it 'stark staring impudence,' and he is absolutely right — it's the philanthropic economy as vanity market.
What Dickens understands is that charity in this world functions not to redistribute wealth but to launder it.
The title of Patron absolves the donor. The poor remain poor. The institution survives.
What strikes me reading Boffin's speech is how Dickens makes the comedy do the work of the argument.
You don't need a lecture on charitable hypocrisy when 'Deceased Patronesses' says it all in two words.
But I want to pull us toward the passages that feel almost unbearably serious — because they're what give the comedy its full meaning.
John Harmon lying in that public-house bed, fevered and half-drowned, thinking — and this is the passage that always stops me —
'the thought entered my head of turning the danger I had passed through, to the account of being for some time supposed to have disappeared mysteriously, and of proving Bella.'
Proving Bella. Two words. And everything is staked on them.
The word 'proving' is doing extraordinary work there, isn't it.
It carries the legal sense — proving a will — which is precisely what Harmon is escaping from.
And it carries the experimental sense — testing, verifying, as you'd prove a mathematical proposition.
But underneath both is something far more vulnerable — the hope that she might prove worthy of being loved.
And from a man who's been dead to the world since childhood — literally parentless, emotionally orphaned — that hope costs everything.
This is the passage where Dickens makes the indictment of money most personal.

Look at how the novel explains Harmon's psychology — 'the distrust engendered by his wretched childhood and the action for evil — never yet for good within his knowledge then — of his father and his father's wealth on all within their influence.'
The wealth acts — it is the active agent, not Harmon's father, not even Harmon himself.
The money has a fate, a gravitational pull toward corruption, and it acts on everyone within its orbit.
What Dickens is saying is that the inheritance system doesn't just distribute gold — it distributes damage.
And what makes it tragic rather than merely polemical is the trap Dickens sets for Harmon — and it's so perfectly designed.
He can come back to life and claim the inheritance — but then he's buying Bella.
Or he can reject the inheritance — but then he's punishing her.
The novel puts it with extraordinary bluntness: 'Was it for him to have the shame of buying her, or the meanness of punishing her?'
Shame. Meanness. Two devastating words on the same scale. Neither option is clean.
And we are made to sit in that impossibility with him, which is exactly what great fiction does.
What I love — and this is the performer in me speaking — is the architecture of the original deception.
Harmon and Radfoot hatching this scheme aboard ship — two men who barely know each other, bonded by circumstance and that peculiar shipboard intimacy.
And the plan itself has this wonderfully innocent impracticality about it — listen to what they actually propose:

'the plot was made out of our getting common sailors' dresses (as he was able to guide me about London), and throwing ourselves in Bella Wilfer's neighbourhood, and trying to put ourselves in her way.'
Throwing themselves in her way! There's something almost touchingly clumsy about it — this is not the plan of a calculating man.
It's the plan of someone who has never learned how to simply want something without engineering elaborate permission.
That detail about the sailors' dresses is worth pausing on — because it's about class disguise.
Harmon is an heir to a fortune built on dust — on the labour of the very poor — and he must dress as the poor to see the woman he's been assigned to marry.
The novel's whole obsession with disguise and false identity is really an obsession with how class is costume — it can be put on and taken off.
But the money underneath doesn't change. The fortune waits. It always waits.
That image of the fortune waiting — the inheritance as something with its own sinister patience — is one that haunts the whole novel.
What's remarkable is that Dickens can make us laugh at Boffin's list of Patronesses in one breath, and feel the full weight of Harmon's impossible dilemma in the next.
The comedy and the tragedy are not separate compartments — they are the same vision of a world distorted by wealth.
In our next segment, we'll be looking at the river itself — what it means, what it carries, and what it refuses to give back.

segments.title: Closing: The Dust Settles—Love, Money, and Redemption

utterances.text: We've arrived at the end of our journey through Our Mutual Friend — and what a journey it has been.
We began in the mud of the Thames, and we close, I think, somewhere closer to the light.
This final segment is our chance to step back and ask what the novel ultimately argues about love, money, and the possibility of redemption.
Daniel, I want to start with you — because Dickens gives us a passage near the end that reads almost like a manifesto.
It concerns the Boffins, these so-called ignorant and unpolished people, and what their goodness actually means in the economy of the novel.
Yes — and the passage is remarkable precisely because Dickens frames it as a law, a structural principle, not just a moral sentiment.
He tells us that the Boffins have guided themselves by a religious sense of duty and desire to do right.
And crucially, the hard wrathful nature that exploited them — old Harmon — could never quite corrupt what it recognised as their moral straightness.
Then he reaches the line that has stayed with me since I first read it.
"For, Evil often stops short at itself and dies with the doer of it; but Good, never."
That word 'never' — placed at the end like a full stop nailed into the wall — that is Dickens at his most uncompromising.
It's a radical claim: that goodness is structurally immortal in a way that evil is not.
What strikes me is the word 'eternal' just before that sentence — 'this is the eternal law.'
Dickens isn't hedging. He isn't saying 'perhaps' or 'one hopes.' He's legislating.
And the Boffins have earned that declaration, I think.
They've absorbed the worst the system could do — old Harmon's grinding meanness — and emerged with their kindness intact.
There's something almost unbearably moving about that. Goodness persisting not despite the pressure but through it.
And yet Dickens doesn't let us wallow in sentiment — he immediately reminds us of the comic absurdity waiting outside the Boffins' door.
Because the moment the Golden Dustman's fortune becomes known, the wolves arrive — all carrying envelopes sealed with ducal coronets.
Listen to this — this is the Secretary reading through the morning post on behalf of the Boffins.
"Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet."
Six words — and Dickens has already punctured the entire aristocratic philanthropy racket.
The Duke of Linseed condescends to invite Boffin to become a Steward — at a personal cost of three guineas.
Dickens notes it is 'friendly' of the Duke — and 'thoughtful in the postscript.' The irony is so dry it crackles.
That passage is doing something more precise than simple satire, though.
Dickens calls it dust for ocular use offered in exchange for the gold dust of the Golden Dustman.
Every charity letter is a commodity transaction dressed in moral language — benevolence as a mechanism of extraction.
And the lithographed letter — printed by the hundred, filled in by another hand — exposes the whole performance.
There is no Duke of Linseed writing warmly to Nicodemus Boffin. There is a printing press targeting a name on a list.
Which brings us, perhaps, to what the novel finally proposes as an alternative to all this corruption.
Caroline — there's a passage involving Bella and John Rokesmith and her father that I think answers that question with remarkable warmth.
It's one of my favourite passages in the entire novel. Bella, John, and dear R. Wilfer — Bella's gentle, hopeless father — sharing a modest supper.
And Dickens reaches for a fairy-tale register to describe it — which tells you everything about what he thinks happiness is.
The passage reads — and I want to read this carefully —

"It was, as Bella gaily said, like the supper provided for the three nursery hobgoblins at their house in the forest, without their thunderous low growlings of the alarming discovery, 'Somebody's been drinking my milk!'"
"It was a delicious repast; by far the most delicious that Bella, or John Rokesmith, or even R. Wilfer had ever made."
'By far the most delicious that any of them had ever made.' Not the grandest. Not the costliest. The most delicious.
The measure of happiness here is entirely internal — nothing to do with what the world assigns as value.
And the detail about the iron safe — two brass knobs staring from the corner like the eyes of some dull dragon — is perfect Dickens.
The money is still present, watching — but it has been domesticated. It cannot touch what's happening at that table.
And Bella 'gaily said' — that word 'gaily' has done an enormous amount of work over the course of this novel.
She began as someone who measured everything by money and social position. Now she's measuring by joy.
I want to hold onto that transformation for a moment, because it matters whether we read it as genuine or as a kind of ideological consolation.
Bella's arc — from mercenary girl to contented wife — is the novel's central act of redemption.
But I think Dickens earns it, partly because he never entirely lets go of the satirical frame.
The Veneerings, the Duke of Linseed, the whole apparatus of wealth and display — none of that is redeemed.
What Dickens is proposing is not that money becomes good. It's that particular people, in particular relationships, can escape its logic.
And that escape — that small, warm supper with brass-knobbed eyes watching from the corner — is all the utopia Dickens allows himself.
And even the Harmon will itself — which drove the whole machinery of the plot — ends with a kind of bleak comedy.
Wegg discovers an earlier will that reads — and I find this wonderful —

"Inasmuch as he has never made friends, and has ever had a rebellious family, he, John Harmon, gives to Nicodemus Boffin the Little Mound, which is quite enough for him, and gives the whole rest and residue of his property to the Crown."
'Never made friends. Ever had a rebellious family.' The elder Harmon's contempt radiates from beyond the grave.
And yet out of that contempt — that loveless, monomaniacal hoarding — the entire novel blossomed.
It's worth noting that Wegg, of all people, is the one reading this document — and he does it with boundless self-congratulation.
'I see I take you with me! Hear, hear, hear!' — this is a man delivering what he believes is a devastating checkmate.
And of course Wegg is about to discover that he has outsmarted absolutely nobody — least of all Mr Boffin.
There's real pleasure in the way Dickens assigns his great comic monsters the most magnificent self-defeats.
We've ranged, in this episode, from the river mud to the supper table, from the worst of London's greed to the best of its human warmth.
And I keep returning to that line Daniel read — 'Good, never.'
Two words. The whole weight of the novel behind them.
My deepest thanks to Oliver Trevelyan, Daniel Rosen, and Caroline Woodcourt — three readers who have made this novel live again today.
Our Mutual Friend rewards every re-reading — and I hope this conversation has sent you straight back to it.
Until next time.

When I devised this story, I foresaw the likelihood that a class of
      readers and commentators would suppose that I was at great pains to
      conceal exactly what I was at great pains to suggest: namely, that Mr John
      Harmon was not slain, and that Mr John Rokesmith was he. Pleasing myself
      with the idea that the supposition might in part arise out of some
      ingenuity in the story, and thinking it worth while, in the interests of
      art, to hint to an audience that an artist (of whatever denomination) may
      perhaps be trusted to know what he is about in his vocation, if they will
      concede him a little patience, I was not alarmed by the anticipation.

      when we come to take it to pieces, bit by bit, where’s the
      satisfactoriness of the money as yet? When the old man does right the poor
      boy after all, the poor boy gets no good of it. He gets made away with, at
      the moment when he’s lifting (as one may say) the cup and sarser to his
      lips. Mr Lightwood, I will now name to you, that on behalf of the poor
      dear boy, me and Mrs Boffin have stood out against the old man times out
      of number, till he has called us every name he could lay his tongue to. I
      have seen him, after Mrs Boffin has given him her mind respecting the
      claims of the nat’ral affections, catch off Mrs Boffin’s bonnet (she wore,
      in general, a black straw, perched as a matter of convenience on the top
      of her head), and send it spinning across the yard. I have indeed. And
      once, when he did this in a manner that amounted to personal, I should
      have given him a rattler for himself, if Mrs Boffin hadn’t thrown herself
      betwixt us, and received flush on the temple. Which dropped her, Mr
      Lightwood. Dropped her.’

      where you changed your clothes, and hid your clothes. I see you with my

      to any one as might come by. I see you rise up Bradley Headstone, Master,
      where you sat down Bargeman. I see you pitch your Bargeman’s bundle into

There was an innocent piece of dinner-furniture that went upon easy
      castors and was kept over a livery stable-yard in Duke Street, Saint
      James’s, when not in use, to whom the Veneerings were a source of blind
      confusion. The name of this article was Twemlow. Being first cousin to
      Lord Snigsworth, he was in frequent requisition, and at many houses might
      be said to represent the dining-table in its normal state. Mr and Mrs
      Veneering, for example, arranging a dinner, habitually started with
      Twemlow, and then put leaves in him, or added guests to him. Sometimes,
      the table consisted of Twemlow and half a dozen leaves; sometimes, of
      Twemlow and a dozen leaves; sometimes, Twemlow was pulled out to his
      utmost extent of twenty leaves. Mr and Mrs Veneering on occasions of
      ceremony faced each other in the centre of the board, and thus the
      parallel still held; for, it always happened that the more Twemlow was
      pulled out, the further he found himself from the center, and nearer to
      the sideboard at one end of the room, or the window-curtains at the other.

      from the still anxious face of that good woman and her obvious wish to
      excuse her husband. ‘Why, what need to excuse him?’ thought Bella, sitting
      down in her own room. ‘What he said was very sensible, I am sure, and very

      came to know it, Charley. The father is like his own father, a weak

      workman too, at the work he does. The mother is dead. This poor ailing
      little creature has come to be what she is, surrounded by drunken people
      from her cradle—if she ever had one, Charley.’

c57:p52.text:
The miserable man whom he had released for the time, but not for long,
      went on towards London. Bradley was suspicious of every sound he heard,
      and of every face he saw, but was under a spell which very commonly falls
      upon the shedder of blood, and had no suspicion of the real danger that
      lurked in his life, and would have it yet. Riderhood was much in his
      thoughts—had never been out of his thoughts since the
      night-adventure of their first meeting; but Riderhood occupied a very
      different place there, from the place of pursuer; and Bradley had been at
      the pains of devising so many means of fitting that place to him, and of
      wedging him into it, that his mind could not compass the possibility of
      his occupying any other. And this is another spell against which the
      shedder of blood for ever strives in vain. There are fifty doors by which
      discovery may enter. With infinite pains and cunning, he double locks and
      bars forty-nine of them, and cannot see the fiftieth standing wide open.

      chest—‘This fellow presumes on my having selected him out of all the

Wegg had repeated the word with a sneer, and was entering on some
      sarcastic retort, when, to his boundless amazement, he found himself
      gripped by the cravat; shaken until his teeth chattered; shoved back,
      staggering, into a corner of the room; and pinned there.

c30:p17.text:
‘I had drank some coffee, when to my sense of sight he began to swell
      immensely, and something urged me to rush at him. We had a struggle near
      the door. He got from me, through my not knowing where to strike, in the
      whirling round of the room, and the flashing of flames of fire between us.
      I dropped down. Lying helpless on the ground, I was turned over by a foot.
      I was dragged by the neck into a corner. I heard men speak together. I was
      turned over by other feet. I saw a figure like myself lying dressed in my
      clothes on a bed. What might have been, for anything I knew, a silence of
      days, weeks, months, years, was broken by a violent wrestling of men all
      over the room. The figure like myself was assailed, and my valise was in
      its hand. I was trodden upon and fallen over. I heard a noise of blows,
      and thought it was a wood-cutter cutting down a tree. I could not have
      said that my name was John Harmon—I could not have thought it—I
      didn’t know it—but when I heard the blows, I thought of the
      wood-cutter and his axe, and had some dead idea that I was lying in a
      forest.

c9:p30.text:
Through his most inveterate purposes, the dead Jailer of Harmony Jail had
      known these two faithful servants to be honest and true. While he raged at
      them and reviled them for opposing him with the speech of the honest and
      true, it had scratched his stony heart, and he had perceived the
      powerlessness of all his wealth to buy them if he had addressed himself to
      the attempt. So, even while he was their griping taskmaster and never gave
      them a good word, he had written their names down in his will. So, even
      while it was his daily declaration that he mistrusted all mankind—and
      sorely indeed he did mistrust all who bore any resemblance to himself—he
      was as certain that these two people, surviving him, would be trustworthy
      in all things from the greatest to the least, as he was that he must
      surely die.
c9:p30.summary: Dickens explains that old John Harmon, despite his misanthropy and greed, respected the Boffins' moral integrity so deeply that he named them in his will as trustees of his fortune.
c9:p30.best_quote: he had perceived the powerlessness of all his wealth to buy them if he had addressed himself to the attempt

c17:p5.text:
These are the corporate beggars. But there are, besides, the individual
      beggars; and how does the heart of the Secretary fail him when he has to
      cope with  them!  And they must be coped with to some extent, because they
      all enclose documents (they call their scraps documents; but they are, as
      to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf), the
      non-return of which would be their ruin. That is to say, they are utterly
      ruined now, but they would be more utterly ruined then. Among these
      correspondents are several daughters of general officers, long accustomed
      to every luxury of life (except spelling), who little thought, when their
      gallant fathers waged war in the Peninsula, that they would ever have to
      appeal to those whom Providence, in its inscrutable wisdom, has blessed
      with untold gold, and from among whom they select the name of Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire, for a maiden effort in this wise, understanding that he
      has such a heart as never was. The Secretary learns, too, that confidence
      between man and wife would seem to obtain but rarely when virtue is in
      distress, so numerous are the wives who take up their pens to ask Mr
      Boffin for money without the knowledge of their devoted husbands, who
      would never permit it; while, on the other hand, so numerous are the
      husbands who take up their pens to ask Mr Boffin for money without the
      knowledge of their devoted wives, who would instantly go out of their
      senses if they had the least suspicion of the circumstance. There are the
      inspired beggars, too. These were sitting, only yesterday evening, musing
      over a fragment of candle which must soon go out and leave them in the
      dark for the rest of their nights, when surely some Angel whispered the
      name of Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, to their souls, imparting rays of hope,
      nay confidence, to which they had long been strangers! Akin to these are
      the suggestively-befriended beggars. They were partaking of a cold potato
      and water by the flickering and gloomy light of a lucifer-match, in their
      lodgings (rent considerably in arrear, and heartless landlady threatening
      expulsion ‘like a dog’ into the streets), when a gifted friend happening
      to look in, said, ‘Write immediately to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire,’ and
      would take no denial. There are the nobly independent beggars too. These,
      in the days of their abundance, ever regarded gold as dross, and have not
      yet got over that only impediment in the way of their amassing wealth, but
      they want no dross from Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire; No, Mr Boffin; the
      world may term it pride, paltry pride if you will, but they wouldn’t take
      it if you offered it; a loan, sir—for fourteen weeks to the day,
      interest calculated at the rate of five per cent per annum, to be bestowed
      upon any charitable institution you may name—is all they want of
      you, and if you have the meanness to refuse it, count on being despised by
      these great spirits. There are the beggars of punctual business-habits
      too. These will make an end of themselves at a quarter to one P.M. on
      Tuesday, if no Post-office order is in the interim received from Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire; arriving after a quarter to one P.M. on Tuesday, it need
      not be sent, as they will then (having made an exact memorandum of the
      heartless circumstances) be ‘cold in death.’ There are the beggars on
      horseback too, in another sense from the sense of the proverb. These are
      mounted and ready to start on the highway to affluence. The goal is before
      them, the road is in the best condition, their spurs are on, the steed is
      willing, but, at the last moment, for want of some special thing—a
      clock, a violin, an astronomical telescope, an electrifying machine—they
      must dismount for ever, unless they receive its equivalent in money from
      Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire. Less given to detail are the beggars who make
      sporting ventures. These, usually to be addressed in reply under initials
      at a country post-office, inquire in feminine hands, Dare one who cannot
      disclose herself to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, but whose name might
      startle him were it revealed, solicit the immediate advance of two hundred
      pounds from unexpected riches exercising their noblest privilege in the
      trust of a common humanity?
c17:p5.summary: The Secretary catalogs individual beggars seeking Boffin's charity—daughters of officers, distressed wives and husbands, those claiming divine inspiration, independent beggars offering loans, and those threatening suicide—each category satirically anatomized.
c17:p5.best_quote: they call their scraps documents; but they are, as to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf

c64:p101.text:
‘Now, scoundrel,’ he pursued, ‘I am going to finish. You supposed me just
      now, to be the possessor of my father’s property.—So I am. But
      through any act of my father’s, or by any right I have? No. Through the
      munificence of Mr Boffin. The conditions that he made with me, before
      parting with the secret of the Dutch bottle, were, that I should take the
      fortune, and that he should take his Mound and no more. I owe everything I
      possess, solely to the disinterestedness, uprightness, tenderness,
      goodness (there are no words to satisfy me) of Mr and Mrs Boffin. And
      when, knowing what I knew, I saw such a mud-worm as you presume to rise in
      this house against this noble soul, the wonder is,’ added John Harmon
      through his clenched teeth, and with a very ugly turn indeed on Wegg’s
      cravat, ‘that I didn’t try to twist your head off, and fling  that  out of
      window! So. That’s the last short speech, do you understand?’
c64:p101.summary: Harmon explains that he owes his fortune entirely to Boffin's generosity, and his fury at Wegg's presumption against such a noble soul.
c64:p101.best_quote: I owe everything I possess, solely to the disinterestedness, uprightness, tenderness, goodness (there are no words to satisfy me) of Mr and Mrs Boffin.

c27:p51.text:
The consideration of Mrs Boffin had clothed Mr Sloppy in a suit of black,
      on which the tailor had received personal directions from Rokesmith to
      expend the utmost cunning of his art, with a view to the concealment of
      the cohering and sustaining buttons. But, so much more powerful were the
      frailties of Sloppy’s form than the strongest resources of tailoring
      science, that he now stood before the Council, a perfect Argus in the way
      of buttons: shining and winking and gleaming and twinkling out of a
      hundred of those eyes of bright metal, at the dazzled spectators. The
      artistic taste of some unknown hatter had furnished him with a hatband of
      wholesale capacity which was fluted behind, from the crown of his hat to
      the brim, and terminated in a black bunch, from which the imagination
      shrunk discomfited and the reason revolted. Some special powers with which
      his legs were endowed, had already hitched up his glossy trousers at the
      ankles, and bagged them at the knees; while similar gifts in his arms had
      raised his coat-sleeves from his wrists and accumulated them at his
      elbows. Thus set forth, with the additional embellishments of a very
      little tail to his coat, and a yawning gulf at his waistband, Sloppy stood
      confessed.
c27:p51.summary: Sloppy's new black suit is a comedic disaster: buttons gleam like eyes, the hatband is absurdly fluted, his sleeves ride up and trousers bag at the knees, and his coat has a yawning gap at the waistband.
c27:p51.best_quote: he now stood before the Council, a perfect Argus in the way of buttons: shining and winking and gleaming and twinkling out of a hundred of those eyes of bright metal, at the dazzled spectators.

c65:p104.text:
Not one other word did Bradley utter all that night. Not once did he
      change his attitude, or loosen his hold upon his wrist. Rigid before the
      fire, as if it were a charmed flame that was turning him old, he sat, with
      the dark lines deepening in his face, its stare becoming more and more
      haggard, its surface turning whiter and whiter as if it were being
      overspread with ashes, and the very texture and colour of his hair
      degenerating.
c65:p104.summary: Bradley sits all night in rigid despair, his face aging, whitening, and degenerating as if being consumed by internal fire while Riderhood maintains his vigilance.

c31:p109.text:
‘I don’t. And if  they  do, my dear, they ought to learn better,’ said Mr
      Boffin. ‘Patrons and Patronesses, and Vice-Patrons and Vice-Patronesses,
      and Deceased Patrons and Deceased Patronesses, and Ex-Vice-Patrons and
      Ex-Vice-Patronesses, what does it all mean in the books of the Charities
      that come pouring in on Rokesmith as he sits among ’em pretty well up to
      his neck! If Mr Tom Noakes gives his five shillings ain’t he a Patron, and
      if Mrs Jack Styles gives her five shillings ain’t she a Patroness? What
      the deuce is it all about? If it ain’t stark staring impudence, what do
      you call it?’
c31:p109.summary: Mr Boffin delivers a scathing critique of the proliferation of patronage titles and the pretension of charity donors who expect public recognition for their contributions.

c30:p22.text:
‘I have checked the calculation often, and it must have been two nights
      that I lay recovering in that public-house. Let me see. Yes. I am sure it
      was while I lay in that bed there, that the thought entered my head of
      turning the danger I had passed through, to the account of being for some
      time supposed to have disappeared mysteriously, and of proving Bella. The
      dread of our being forced on one another, and perpetuating the fate that
      seemed to have fallen on my father’s riches—the fate that they
      should lead to nothing but evil—was strong upon the moral timidity
      that dates from my childhood with my poor sister.
c30:p22.summary: While recovering in the public-house, John Harmon decides to let himself remain dead for a time to prove Bella's character and avoid perpetuating his father's wealth's curse.
c30:p22.best_quote: the thought entered my head of turning the danger I had passed through, to the account of being for some time supposed to have disappeared mysteriously, and of proving Bella

c31:p1.text:
He went over it all again. He had lapsed into the condition in which he
      found himself, as many a man lapses into many a condition, without
      perceiving the accumulative power of its separate circumstances. When in
      the distrust engendered by his wretched childhood and the action for evil—never
      yet for good within his knowledge then—of his father and his
      father’s wealth on all within their influence, he conceived the idea of
      his first deception, it was meant to be harmless, it was to last but a few
      hours or days, it was to involve in it only the girl so capriciously
      forced upon him and upon whom he was so capriciously forced, and it was
      honestly meant well towards her. For, if he had found her unhappy in the
      prospect of that marriage (through her heart inclining to another man or
      for any other cause), he would seriously have said: ‘This is another of
      the old perverted uses of the misery-making money. I will let it go to my
      and my sister’s only protectors and friends.’ When the snare into which he
      fell so outstripped his first intention as that he found himself placarded
      by the police authorities upon the London walls for dead, he confusedly
      accepted the aid that fell upon him, without considering how firmly it
      must seem to fix the Boffins in their accession to the fortune. When he
      saw them, and knew them, and even from his vantage-ground of inspection
      could find no flaw in them, he asked himself, ‘And shall I come to life to
      dispossess such people as these?’ There was no good to set against the
      putting of them to that hard proof. He had heard from Bella’s own lips
      when he stood tapping at the door on that night of his taking the
      lodgings, that the marriage would have been on her part thoroughly
      mercenary. He had since tried her, in his own unknown person and supposed
      station, and she not only rejected his advances but resented them. Was it
      for him to have the shame of buying her, or the meanness of punishing her?
      Yet, by coming to life and accepting the condition of the inheritance, he
      must do the former; and by coming to life and rejecting it, he must do the
      latter.
c31:p1.summary: Rokesmith justifies his original deception as harmless, traces how it spiralled beyond his control, and wrestles with the impossible choice between disgracing Bella or deceiving the Boffins.
c31:p1.best_quote: When in the distrust engendered by his wretched childhood and the action for evil—never yet for good within his knowledge then—of his father and his father's wealth on all within their influence, he conceived the idea of his first deception, it was meant to be harmless, it was to last but a few hours or days.

c30:p9.text:
‘However, a sociable word or two on these mistakes became an easy
      introduction between us, and the weather was hot, and he helped me to a
      cool cabin on deck alongside his own, and his first school had been at
      Brussels as mine had been, and he had learnt French as I had learnt it,
      and he had a little history of himself to relate—God only knows how
      much of it true, and how much of it false—that had its likeness to
      mine. I had been a seaman too. So we got to be confidential together, and
      the more easily yet, because he and every one on board had known by
      general rumour what I was making the voyage to England for. By such
      degrees and means, he came to the knowledge of my uneasiness of mind, and
      of its setting at that time in the direction of desiring to see and form
      some judgment of my allotted wife, before she could possibly know me for
      myself; also to try Mrs Boffin and give her a glad surprise. So the plot
      was made out of our getting common sailors’ dresses (as he was able to
      guide me about London), and throwing ourselves in Bella Wilfer’s
      neighbourhood, and trying to put ourselves in her way, and doing whatever
      chance might favour on the spot, and seeing what came of it. If nothing
      came of it, I should be no worse off, and there would merely be a short
      delay in my presenting myself to Lightwood. I have all these facts right?
      Yes. They are all accurately right.
c30:p9.summary: John Harmon describes the scheme he and Radfoot devised to dress as common sailors, observe Bella Wilfer, surprise Mrs Boffin, and determine the authenticity of Bella's character before revealing himself to Lightwood.
c30:p9.best_quote: the plot was made out of our getting common sailors' dresses (as he was able to guide me about London), and throwing ourselves in Bella Wilfer's neighbourhood, and trying to put ourselves in her way

c9:p29.text:
These two ignorant and unpolished people had guided themselves so far on
      in their journey of life, by a religious sense of duty and desire to do
      right. Ten thousand weaknesses and absurdities might have been detected in
      the breasts of both; ten thousand vanities additional, possibly, in the
      breast of the woman. But the hard wrathful and sordid nature that had
      wrung as much work out of them as could be got in their best days, for as
      little money as could be paid to hurry on their worst, had never been so
      warped but that it knew their moral straightness and respected it. In its
      own despite, in a constant conflict with itself and them, it had done so.
      And this is the eternal law. For, Evil often stops short at itself and
      dies with the doer of it; but Good, never.
c9:p29.summary: Dickens reflects that the Boffins, though ignorant and unpolished, have been guided by genuine religious duty and moral righteousness that even hardened souls cannot entirely resist.
c9:p29.best_quote: For, Evil often stops short at itself and dies with the doer of it; but Good, never.

c17:p4.text:
But no one knows so well as the Secretary, who opens and reads the
      letters, what a set is made at the man marked by a stroke of notoriety. Oh
      the varieties of dust for ocular use, offered in exchange for the gold
      dust of the Golden Dustman! Fifty-seven churches to be erected with
      half-crowns, forty-two parsonage houses to be repaired with shillings,
      seven-and-twenty organs to be built with halfpence, twelve hundred
      children to be brought up on postage stamps. Not that a half-crown,
      shilling, halfpenny, or postage stamp, would be particularly acceptable
      from Mr Boffin, but that it is so obvious he is the man to make up the
      deficiency. And then the charities, my Christian brother! And mostly in
      difficulties, yet mostly lavish, too, in the expensive articles of print
      and paper. Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.
      ‘Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire. My Dear Sir,—Having consented to preside
      at the forthcoming Annual Dinner of the Family Party Fund, and feeling
      deeply impressed with the immense usefulness of that noble Institution and
      the great importance of its being supported by a List of Stewards that
      shall prove to the public the interest taken in it by popular and
      distinguished men, I have undertaken to ask you to become a Steward on
      that occasion. Soliciting your favourable reply before the 14th instant, I
      am, My Dear Sir, Your faithful Servant,  Linseed . P.S. The Steward’s fee is
      limited to three Guineas.’ Friendly this, on the part of the Duke of
      Linseed (and thoughtful in the postscript), only lithographed by the
      hundred and presenting but a pale individuality of an address to Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire, in quite another hand. It takes two noble Earls and a
      Viscount, combined, to inform Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, in an equally
      flattering manner, that an estimable lady in the West of England has
      offered to present a purse containing twenty pounds, to the Society for
      Granting Annuities to Unassuming Members of the Middle Classes, if twenty
      individuals will previously present purses of one hundred pounds each. And
      those benevolent noblemen very kindly point out that if Nicodemus Boffin,
      Esquire, should wish to present two or more purses, it will not be
      inconsistent with the design of the estimable lady in the West of England,
      provided each purse be coupled with the name of some member of his
      honoured and respected family.
c17:p4.summary: The Secretary describes the flood of charitable solicitations and scheme proposals that inundate the Boffins, including a satirical example of a duke's letter requesting Boffin become a Steward of a charity for a three-guinea fee.
c17:p4.best_quote: Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.

c49:p79.text:
It was, as Bella gaily said, like the supper provided for the three
      nursery hobgoblins at their house in the forest, without their thunderous
      low growlings of the alarming discovery, ‘Somebody’s been drinking  my 
      milk!’ It was a delicious repast; by far the most delicious that Bella, or
      John Rokesmith, or even R. Wilfer had ever made. The uncongenial oddity of

      Veneering, and Stobbles staring from a corner, like the eyes of some dull
      dragon, only made it the more delightful.

c40:p31.text:
‘Exactly so, sir!’ returned Wegg, blandly and buoyantly. ‘I see I take you
      with me! Hear, hear, hear! Resolved, as your discriminating good sense
      perceives, that if you was to have a sap—pur— ize , it should be
      a complete one! Well, sir. And so, as you have honoured me by
      anticipating, I examined the document. Regularly executed, regularly
      witnessed, very short. Inasmuch as he has never made friends, and has ever
      had a rebellious family, he, John Harmon, gives to Nicodemus Boffin the
      Little Mound, which is quite enough for him, and gives the whole rest and
      residue of his property to the Crown.’
